title: Rectified linear units (ReLU)
matchup: Nair and Hinton (2010) and AlexNet (2012) vs Fukushima (1969) and von der Malsburg (1973)
question: Does Fukushima's 1969 activation function establish the ReLU invention priority that Schmidhuber claims for it?

usual_credit.summary: Vinod Nair and Geoffrey Hinton's 2010 paper studied rectified linear units in restricted Boltzmann machines, and the AlexNet paper adopted their terminology for the activation max(0, x). AlexNet reported faster training than with tanh units, helping make rectifiers common in deep convolutional networks. Hinton's Nobel lecture describes Nair and Hinton's work as introducing the nonlinearity, which is the wording Schmidhuber challenges. The credit at issue therefore spans the activation function's earlier appearance, its later probabilistic formulation and its demonstrated usefulness in large modern networks.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says that rectified linear neurons were used by Kunihiko Fukushima in 1969 and that the 2012 AlexNet paper did not cite their origins. He says the same of the 2021 Turing Lecture by LeCun, Bengio and Hinton, which devotes a section to ReLUs citing papers of the 2000s by Hinton and his students. The first version of his critique named Christoph von der Malsburg (1973) as the earlier source, and later versions name Fukushima (1969) and cite both.

response.summary: Nair and Hinton study rectified units in restricted Boltzmann machines, and AlexNet credits their terminology while reporting faster training than with tanh units. The 2010 paper cites Hahnloser and colleagues but not Fukushima or von der Malsburg. The 2016 Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville textbook mentions Fukushima's cognitron as an earlier, more complicated rectifier design and says the simpler modern unit emerged through several viewpoints. These sources distinguish earlier activation functions from later demonstrations of their use, but do not provide a direct answer by Hinton to the specific Fukushima citation complaint.

quotes.text: Following Nair and Hinton [20], we refer to neurons with this nonlinearity as Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs).
introduced rectified linear nonlinearity (Nair and Hinton, 2010)
Most previous studies of neural networks involving a rectifying activation function concern recurrent networks (Salinas and Abbott, 1996; Hahnloser, 1998).
The original cognitron (Fukushima, 1975) introduced a more complicated version that was highly inspired by our knowledge of brain function.
Kunihiko Fukushima in 1969 used ReLU in the context of visual feature extraction in hierarchical neural networks.

agreed_facts: Fukushima published 'Visual feature extraction by a multilayered network of analog threshold elements' in IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics in 1969.
Nair and Hinton presented 'Rectified linear units improve restricted Boltzmann machines' at ICML in 2010, and Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton presented their ImageNet paper at NIPS in 2012.
Neither Nair and Hinton (2010) nor Glorot, Bordes and Bengio (2011) lists Fukushima (1969) among its references.
The 2012 AlexNet paper credits Nair and Hinton for the term Rectified Linear Unit.
crux: The dispute is whether the half-wave rectifier in Fukushima's 1969 analog threshold elements is the same function as the rectified linear unit that Nair and Hinton studied in 2010 for restricted Boltzmann machines and that AlexNet used for deep convolutional networks. It also asks whether the later papers owed a citation to the earlier use, or whether showing that the function speeds up training in a new setting is a separate contribution.
